why: Two rules in `.tick/runners.toml` are enforced by two implementations in two
languages: `[sandbox].image` and `[orchestration].max_parallel`. Go owns the
format (internal/herd/config/load.go); the control plane reads both keys
before any container exists to read anything, so it re-implements them
(cloud/factory/src/repo-config.ts).
Since 4.0.0 the file also pins the document's TABLE ENUMERATION and the
SUBSTRATE ENUM — the split ticfac's epic av8 made (2026-09-10), which until
now was a shape two readers agreed on by comment. The tables section names
which half of `.tick/runners.toml` each reader owns and what it does with the
other half; the substrate section pins the closed vocabulary of
`orchestration.substrate`, which decides which dispatch verb is correct.
Drift here already fails LOUD rather than silent — the sandbox entrypoint
refuses the boot when the image `tk` reads disagrees with the one the control
plane says it booted, and `kji`'s claim-time check inside each worker is the
authoritative wave-width bound no dispatch-side miss can bypass. So this
fixture is not closing a hole; it moves the failure from a container at run
time to a test at edit time.
It pins the RULES. The behaviour of the two image readers over whole TOML
documents is pinned separately, and case by case, in sandbox-image-cases.json.
internal/herd/config/runners_config_parity_test.go asserts this file against
Go's validator; cloud/factory/test/repo-config.test.ts asserts it against the
Worker's reader; and since the split, ticfac's own reader (internal/runconfig,
vendored from this package) asserts the tables and substrate sections through
internal/contracts/parity/runners_config_test.go — the same cases, both sides
of the split, one file.
The pattern string itself is pinned, not just its effect: it is copied
character for character between `imagePattern` in internal/herd/config and
`IMAGE_PATTERN` in cloud/factory/src/repo-config.ts, and Go's
Regexp.String() and JavaScript's RegExp.source render it identically.
Deliberately narrow — an image reference is a name, never a place to hide a
shell fragment.
`max_length` is the schema's bound (`maxImageLen` / `MAX_IMAGE_LENGTH`).
Both sides build a reference of exactly that many `boundary_char`s, which
must be ACCEPTED, and one character more, which must be refused: a bound
pinned only from the outside would not catch an off-by-one.
image.refusal_message: is not a well-formed image reference

why: The wave width a cloud run's container fan-out must not silently exceed
(tick b6e). One bound, `>= 1`, enforced by Go's validator and by the
control plane's reader — and the refusal text is shared too, because the
two answer the same question and a config author should not be able to tell
which one refused.
`refused_toml_values` are raw TOML value texts rather than JSON numbers:
the point of those cases is that a typed value the schema does not allow is
a refusal on both sides, never a coercion, and only the TOML text can carry
the difference between 3, 1.5 and "3".
THE [findings] TABLE. `[findings.route.<owner/name>]` is the explicit,
reviewed authorisation for a run to FILE a finding a worker routed to
ANOTHER repository into that repository's own tracker: until it existed a
routed finding waited for a person and held the close-out (the epic-2jn
stall, 2026-09-27). The allowlist is explicit and per repository on
purpose — pushing to another repository's default branch is a write outside
the run's own tree, and the tracked, PR-reviewed config is the only thing
that may authorise it.
The table joined the format after this file stopped being vendored (ticfac
tick #85), so it was covered only by ticfac's own config tests until ticfac
took this contract over (tick 4i8) and pinned it here. It is ticfac's
alone: the run that routes and files findings is ticfac's
(internal/runconfig, `Findings`/`FindingRoute`), and every case below runs
through that real reader over whole documents.
findings.target_rule: A route's key is a target repository, owner/name — the same spelling a worker's finding carries in its `target`, so a typo'd key is refused rather than filed to.
findings.file_rule: boolean. `true` lets the run file the finding as a tick in the target's own tracker; `false` (or absent) is the documented fallback: a local backlog tick naming the target, so a person finds it in the tracker they already read.
findings.remote_rule: The git URL the target is fetched from and pushed to. Absent derives it from this repository's own remote with the owner/name replaced; present, it must be a place, never an option: non-empty, no leading '-', no whitespace or control characters.

accepted.name: two routes, one derived remote
accepted.why: The shape the table exists for: one target filed in its own tracker, one with an explicit remote. Both load; an undeclared target answers no route at all — the allowlist is explicit, not a pattern.
accepted.toml:
version = 2

[roles.implement]
kind = "claude"

[findings.route."pengelbrecht/ticks"]
file = true

[findings.route."example/elsewhere"]
file = false
remote = "git@example.com:example/elsewhere.git"

refused.name: a target that is not owner/name
refused.why: The key is the repository a finding is pushed to; anything that is not owner/name is a typo a run would otherwise push to, and the refusal names the shape.
refused.expect_error_contains: is not a repository a finding can be routed to

refused.name: a remote git would read as an option
refused.why: The remote is handed to git as an argument, so a leading '-' must never reach it: `--upload-pack` is a command, not a place.
refused.toml:
version = 2

[roles.implement]
kind = "claude"

[findings.route."a/b"]
file = true
remote = "--upload-pack=touch x"

refused.name: an empty remote
refused.why: Empty is not "derive" — derivation is the ABSENT key, so an explicit empty string is refused rather than half-deriving.

refused.name: a remote with whitespace
refused.why: A URL with a space in it is not a place git recognises, and whitespace is how a second argument hides inside one.
refused.toml:
version = 2

[roles.implement]
kind = "claude"

[findings.route."a/b"]
file = true
remote = "git@x:a/b c"

refused.name: a typo'd key inside a route
refused.why: The route's key vocabulary is closed: `fiel = true` is a typo, not a future key, and unknown keys fail closed as everywhere else in this document.

refused.name: a file flag that is not a boolean
refused.why: `file = "yes"` is a string where a boolean is declared; a reader that coerced it would turn a typo into an authorisation.

why: THE TABLE ENUMERATION (4.0.0). `.tick/runners.toml` is ONE document with TWO
domains and TWO readers, and until this section the split lived in comments on
both sides — the shape a reader agrees on with itself, which is what bundle
1.2.0 shipped for the evidence record. The execution tables belong to ticfac's
orchestrator (its internal/runconfig, lifted from this repository's
internal/herd/config); the tracker tables are ticks' own, acted on by the cloud
factory's control plane with tk as their author-time validator. ONE writer stays:
ticks' migrator (`tk config migrate`), so a file written by the other side's
migrator cannot exist.
The tolerance rule is keyed on SHAPE, not on the bare name. A reader pinned to
its own half meets the other half's tables as TABLES — neither validated nor
refused, because a legal file on the other side of the split is not a typo'd key
on this side. A SCALAR squatting on a foreign table's name has no table shape, so
the tolerance never fires: it is refused as an unknown key exactly as if it were
misspelled. A refusal is the one thing a foreign table may never cause, and a
scalar on its name is not a foreign table.
The mirror obligation runs both ways, and both directions are pinned by the
cases below: ticfac's reader tolerates `[signals]` and `[sweeps]`; THIS reader
tolerates `[tier_policy]` — ticfac's tier ladder (its tick 5eq), a table ticks
will never own the semantics of — because a repository that declares it is a
legal file on this reader's half too. When ticks retires its execution machinery
(ticfac tick 4l2) the remaining execution tables become foreign here the same
way; this enumeration is what makes that a pin bump on both sides, never a
silent refusal of a repository's good file.
READERS: internal/herd/config/runners_config_parity_test.go runs every case
whose `readers` names this repository; ticfac's internal/contracts/parity/
runners_config_test.go runs every case whose `readers` names ticfac. An
`accepted` case with both readers listed must load in BOTH, so a table added to
one half fails the other side's build, not its own.
tables.version_rule: The version key is the one property of the WHOLE document, gated by both readers before shape: a file from a future format version is refused with one upgrade line, never with a list of unknown keys.
tables.execution_owner: ticfac (internal/runconfig, lifted from this repository's internal/herd/config); this repository's reader still validates the shared half until it retires its execution machinery (ticfac tick 4l2)
tables.tracker_owner: ticks: the cloud factory's control plane acts on them and tk is their author-time validator
tables.foreign_table_rule: A table from the other reader's half is tolerated when present as a table, neither validated nor refused; a scalar squatting on its name is a typo'd key and refused as unknown.

accepted.name: every execution table, one document
accepted.why: The whole execution half, one working file. Both readers load it: this one still validates every table, ticfac's owns them.
accepted.toml:
version = 2

[orchestrator]
kind = "claude"

[orchestration]
substrate = "auto"
detect = "env-or-socket"
max_parallel = 4

[roles.implement]
kind = "claude"
model = "opus"

[roles.implement.tiers.economy]
model = "haiku"

[testing.commands]
go = { command = "go test ./...", description = "Go" }

[evidence.commands]
audit = { command = "go vet ./...", description = "Close-out audit" }

[environment.commands]
toolchain = { command = "which go", description = "Go toolchain on PATH" }

[sandbox]
image = "ticks-orchestrator:0.32.0"

accepted.name: the tracker tables beside a working execution config
accepted.why: The file both readers exist for: a repository that declares both halves. This reader validates the tracker tables; ticfac's tolerates them as foreign tables, which is the split working, not the split failing.

accepted.name: the tier_policy table, which ticks will never own
accepted.why: THE MIRROR TOLERANCE. ticfac's reader validates [tier_policy] in full; this reader tolerates it as a foreign table, so a repository that declares its own tier ladder is a legal file here too.
accepted.toml:
version = 2

[roles.implement]
kind = "claude"

[tier_policy]
default = "strong"
ceiling = "frontier"
step = 1

[[tier_policy.start]]
tier = "economy"
types = ["bug"]

[tier_policy.roles]
review-epic = "strong"

refused.name: a typo'd execution table name
refused.why: additionalProperties: false on the shared half: an unknown TABLE is an error on both readers, never silently ignored — the split pins what each half owns, not what it tolerates.

refused.name: a typo'd execution key inside a table
refused.why: The tolerance never extends to a key INSIDE a table this reader owns: a typo'd substrate key must not hide behind the split.

refused.name: a scalar squatting on a tracker table's name, read by the execution half
refused.why: The tolerance is keyed on shape, not name: `signals = true` is not the tracker table [signals], it is a typo'd key in a file this reader owns nothing of, and it is refused. (This repository's reader decodes [signals] as its own table, so the same text is a type error there — which is also a refusal.)

refused.name: a scalar squatting on the tier_policy name, read by the tracker half
refused.why: The mirror of the same rule: this reader has no [tier_policy] field, so `tier_policy = true` is a typo'd key here — while in ticfac's reader the same line is a type error against a table it owns. Both refuse; neither falls back to defaults.

why: THE SUBSTRATE ENUM (4.0.0). `[orchestration].substrate` decides which
substrate orchestrates a run, and therefore which dispatch verb is correct: a
cloud run must refuse `tk herd spawn`, and a herdr run that degrades to harness
orchestration must SAY so rather than fail. The four values are a closed enum, not
free text, because a substrate a reader cannot parse authorises nothing — a run
that fell back to the file's default after being told a substrate is the exact
failure the value exists to prevent (the container case: a cloud sandbox has no
herdr server and never will).
`herdr` — workers are herdr panes/worktrees; an unavailable herdr is an explicit
degradation to harness orchestration, never a failed run. `harness` — the
harness's own subagents, always; terminal, never probed for herdr. `auto` — the
default: herdr when it is there, harness when it is not, and neither is a
failure. `cloud` — one cloud sandbox per tick through the run API; terminal,
never probed, and no local worktree ever appears for a tick until its container
pushes one.
The same vocabulary governs the environment override (`TICKS_SUBSTRATE`), which
is how whatever boots a run states the substrate that is effective where the run
actually executes. The override refuses a value outside the enum with the same
words, quoted — one vocabulary, two surfaces.
READERS: internal/herd/config/runners_config_parity_test.go (this repository) and
ticfac's internal/contracts/parity/runners_config_test.go, both through their own
real readers over whole documents.
substrate.refusal_message: is not one of herdr, harness, auto, cloud
